extracted.intended_audience: corporate communications professionals, investor-relations teams, financial PR writers, and financial-text analysts
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and writing earnings/financial press releases so their lexical tone is correctly interpreted by human analysts and algorithmic news/ trading systems, using Loughran & McDonald domain-specific word lists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Domain-correct tone audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Loughran-McDonald financial dictionary, not general-purpose sentiment lexicons, when auditing release tone — analysts and algorithms increasingly do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General-purpose dictionaries (e.g., Harvard IV-4) systematically misclassify financial language (in 10-Ks ~75% of words flagged 'negative' by Harvard are not negative in financial context). Use L-M lists (negative, positive, uncertainty, litigious, modal-strong, modal-weak) as the domain-appropriate lexicon when measuring or crafting tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Negative-word minimization (where genuine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Words on the L-M negative list (e.g., 'loss', 'decline', 'litigation', 'impairment') will be picked up by algorithmic readers and amplify negative coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include negative words only when required by the underlying fact. Excess or unnecessary negative wording increases the chance of amplified negative algorithmic scoring and adverse analyst/media reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Litigious-word screen
rubrics_metrics.description: L-M's 'litigious' list flags legal-exposure language; overuse in releases attracts lawyer-side scrutiny and analyst downgrades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use legal/litigious vocabulary precisely and only where disclosure obligations require it. Unwarranted use can trigger heightened attention from legal teams and negative market interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uncertainty-word calibration
rubrics_metrics.description: L-M's 'uncertainty' list (examples: 'approximately', 'could', 'may') is associated with higher return volatility around announcements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use uncertainty markers only when truly warranted; avoid padding releases with hedging language that signals unknowns to algorithmic and human readers and can increase volatility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modal-strong vs. modal-weak
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish modal-strong ('will', 'must', 'shall') which signal commitment from modal-weak ('may', 'might', 'could') which signal hedging; over-reliance on modal-weak phrases signals evasiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose modality deliberately: modal-weak language can cause algorithms and analysts to downgrade perceived certainty or management commitment. Use stronger modals when commitment is intended and factually supported; hedge only when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Algorithm-readability awareness
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern earnings-release pickup includes algorithmic news consumers (e.g., high-frequency-trading text-analytics pipelines); these systems materially influence market reaction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write releases with awareness that algorithms parse and score tone; failures to account for how algorithms tokenize, weight, and interpret words/phrases will cause underperformance versus peers and unintended market moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verb-tense disambiguation
rubrics_metrics.description: Past-tense factual statements versus forward-looking statements should be lexically distinguishable to avoid algorithmic mis-tagging.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make forward-looking language explicitly marked (and/or placed in appropriate boilerplate/forward-looking sections) and keep factual past-tense reporting clearly distinct so automated taggers do not conflate assertions and projections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentence-length control
rubrics_metrics.description: Algorithmic parsers favor short sentences; long sentences with embedded clauses are more likely to be mis-parsed and mis-scored for tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer shorter, simple sentences for key assertions (headline, lead, key facts) to reduce parser errors. Break up long, embedded clauses that could confuse tokenization or sentiment assignment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal-consistency check
rubrics_metrics.description: Tone in headline, lead, and body should converge; algorithms compute weighted-tone scores across sections so inconsistency triggers anomaly flags.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure headline, lead paragraph, and body present a coherent tonal message. Divergent tones across sections can produce algorithmic anomaly flags and unexpected market or media responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: L-M-aware writing as precondition for accurate market reception
rubrics_metrics.description: For financial press releases in the post-2010 algorithmic-trading era, Loughran-McDonald-aware writing is a precondition for accurate market reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A release that fails the domain-correct tone audit will be mis-scored by algorithms and may move the stock in unintended directions; a release that passes the audit is more likely to receive correct pricing and broader pickup by outlets that use L-M tone analytics.
